extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, reporters, and general readers interested in investigative journalism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards for producing and understanding investigative journalism: its definition, typical practices and tools, ethical concerns, historical examples, and institutional contexts. Useful for reporters, students, and editors learning what investigative work entails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — initiative and public importance (Weinberg)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Reporting, through one's own initiative and work product, matters of importance to readers, viewers, or listeners."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigative journalism is characterized by original initiative by the reporter and focuses on matters important to the public; subjects of reporting often prefer matters remain undisclosed. Use this as a primary test of whether work qualifies as investigative reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role — discover truth and identify lapses (de Burgh)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An investigative journalist is ... whose profession is to discover the truth and to identify lapses from it ... distinct from apparently similar work done by police, lawyers, auditors, and regulatory bodies in that it is not limited as to target, not legally founded and closely connected to publicity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes watchdog/accountability function, broad choice of targets, independence from legal or institutional constraints, and a close connection to public exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and duration of investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigative journalist may spend months or years researching and preparing a report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations are typically long-form and resource-intensive; expect extended research, document gathering, interviews, verification, and possible collaboration across time and organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on hidden problems and public-interest topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative journalism deeply investigates topics such as hidden problems and truths, serious crimes, education, racial injustice, corruption and abuse of power, social welfare, and corporate wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select topics with clear public-interest implications and likelihood of uncovering concealed or systemic issues. The aim is accountability and informing the public about significant harms or abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of documentary evidence and document analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of documents, such as lawsuits and other legal documents, tax records, government reports, regulatory reports, and corporate financial filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough document analysis is central: obtain, catalog, and scrutinize primary-source paperwork to corroborate claims and trace behavior; this often requires legal/financial literacy or specialist help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of public-records databases
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage searchable public-records and government databases to find filings, records, property ownership, corporate registrations, licenses, and other documentary leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical and subject-matter investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigation of technical issues, including scrutiny of government and business practices and their effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stories involve technical, scientific, or regulatory subject matter, reporters should perform substantive technical scrutiny or consult experts to interpret complex evidence and impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research into social and legal issues; subscription research sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Research into social and legal issues. Subscription research sources such as LexisNexis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine domain research (law, policy, social science) and paid databases (LexisNexis, archives) to situate findings in context and to retrieve historical or hard-to-find materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interviews — on-the-record and anonymous sources (whistleblowers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous interviews with on-the-record sources as well as, in some instances, interviews with anonymous sources (for example whistleblowers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct many interviews to corroborate documentary evidence. Use anonymous sourcing carefully to protect vulnerable sources and to verify claims through independent corroboration; be mindful of editorial and legal standards for using anonymous testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of Information requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal or state Freedom of Information Acts to obtain documents and data from government agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File FOIA/FOI requests to compel release of government documents; be prepared for delays, exemptions, appeals, and the need to interpret heavily redacted records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) tools
rubrics_metrics.description: OSINT (Open-Source Intelligence) databases and tools that contain free and open resources that anybody can use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ online open-source tools, satellite imagery, social-media traces, registries, and other publicly accessible digital resources to corroborate or refute claims and to generate leads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative and cross-organizational investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic investigations are increasingly carried out by news organizations working together, even internationally (as in the case of the Panama Papers, Paradise Papers and Pandora Papers), or by nonprofit outlets such as ProPublica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, complex investigations may require cross-border collaboration, data-sharing, secure communications, and coordinated publication plans; nonprofits and consortiums can pool resources and expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and safety — source protection, defamation, and reporter safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Ethics and standards: freedom of information, freedom of the press (defamation; safety); source protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize legal risk assessment (defamation), protect confidential sources, adopt digital and physical safety practices for reporters and sources, and follow codes of ethics. Be aware of reprisals and state or corporate pressures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact and accountability as measures of success
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigative reports have historically led to policy or institutional change (examples: Standard Oil dismantling, creation of FDA, resignation of Nixon after Watergate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for verifiable public impact: regulatory, legal, or policy changes, prosecutions, resignations, or public awareness. Impact can serve as a retrospective quality measure but should not replace rigorous standards of verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resource and funding considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: With the decline in income through advertising, many traditional news services have struggled to fund investigative journalism, due to it being very time-consuming and expensive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for sustained funding and resources; consider nonprofit models, grants, partnerships, or consortium approaches to support long-term investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics and formats — undercover, database journalism, long-form
rubrics_metrics.description: Genres and tactics associated with investigative reporting include undercover investigation, computer-assisted reporting (database journalism), long-form, narrative, and immersion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate formats and tactics for the story: undercover work has special ethical/legal considerations; database journalism requires data skills; long-form/narrative pieces suit complex investigations requiring deep explanation.
